name: Likwala
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Louango, Paul. 1989. Esquisse phonologique du likwala. Thesis; Ikemou, R.P. 2017. Elements of Phonology of the Likwala, IJLL 4(3):80-85 (journal site ijllnet.com is dead). Neither reachable.

new_statements.quote: Like the other Bantu C group languages, likwála is a tonal language. That is, it uses the variations of melodic high for lexical and grammatical. Tone is a supra segmental unit, it is as important as the segments. Tone is generally associated to vowels. likwála makes use of two tones, that is the high tone (H) and the low tone (L). These tones are susceptible to appear on any syllable. [...] [abstract, p.80:] likwála is a tonal language with two tones ( High and Low) only.
new_statements.citation: Ikemou, Régina Patience. 2017. Elements of Phonology of the Likwála, Variety of Koyó Ngandza. International Journal of Language and Linguistics 4(3): 80-85.
new_statements.locator: p.85 (tone section, before Conclusion); also abstract p.80
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File is a genuine 6-page text-layer PDF (Word 2007, created 2017-11-16) of Ikemou 2017, IJLL 4(3):80-85, fetched sources from the journal's live open host (ijllnet.thebrpi.org). The quoted passage is present verbatim at p.85, opening the (unnumbered) tone section directly before the Conclusion: 'Like the other Bantu C group languages, likwála is a tonal language. That is, it uses the variations of melodic high for lexical and grammatical. Tone is a supra segmental unit, it is as important as the segments. Tone is generally associated to vowels. likwála makes use of two tones, that is the high tone (H) and the low tone (L). These tones are susceptible to appear on any syllable.' The abstract…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Likwála is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with tones free to occur on any syllable; the description contains no statement about word stress or accent at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding prominence; only notes that the extension-suffix vowel is toneless and receives tone by anticipatory association (Meeussen 1967).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/grammatical tone on the word; 'Tones are steady in the lexicon as in the statement' (p.85 Conclusion). No phrase-level prominence discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Ikemou 2017 describes 'Likwála, variety of Koyó Ngandza' — i.e. Likwala (C26, likw1239) as spoken at Koyó-Ngandza in the Cuvette department east of Owando (per Ikemou & Nzete 2018); explicitly identified by the author as Guthrie C26 / mbochi group C20. Not to be confused with the separate Koyo language (C24, koyo1242), which the same author describes elsewhere (Ikemou 2018, LLA). Nzete 1983 concerns the Bokwele variety of Likwala.

sources.quote: Like the other Bantu C group languages, likwála is a tonal language. That is, it uses the variations of melodic high for lexical and grammatical. Tone is a supra segmental unit, it is as important as the segments. Tone is generally associated to vowels. likwála makes use of two tones, that is the high tone (H) and the low tone (L). These tones are susceptible to appear on any syllable. [...] [abstract, p.80:] likwála is a tonal language with two tones ( High and Low) only.
sources.locator: p.85 (tone section, before Conclusion); also abstract p.80
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. States Likwála is a tonal language with two tones (H, L) which 'are susceptible to appear on any syllable' (p.85; abstract p.80); all syllables open (CV, V).
